claims.claim: Oregon-R flies showed reduced oviposition when exposed to wasps (unexposed ~57 ± 2.84 eggs compared to exposed 13 ± 1.88 eggs on average).
claims.source: We observed this robust response in at least four different genetic backgrounds including Canton-S (CS), Oregon-R (OreR) (unexposed ∼57 ± 2.84 eggs compared to exposed 13 ± 1.88 eggs on average), w1118 (unexposed ∼25 ± 1.54 eggs compared to exposed ∼1 ± 0.53 egg on average), and transgenic flies carrying Histone H2AvD-GFP (His-GFP) (unexposed ∼108 ± 7.69 eggs compared to exposed 18 ± 1.97 eggs) (Clarkson and Saint, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments across multiple genetic backgrounds.

claims.claim: w1118 flies showed reduced oviposition when exposed to wasps (unexposed ~25 ± 1.54 eggs compared to exposed ~1 ± 0.53 egg on average).
claims.source: We observed this robust response in at least four different genetic backgrounds including Canton-S (CS), Oregon-R (OreR) (unexposed ∼57 ± 2.84 eggs compared to exposed 13 ± 1.88 eggs on average), w1118 (unexposed ∼25 ± 1.54 eggs compared to exposed ∼1 ± 0.53 egg on average), and transgenic flies carrying Histone H2AvD-GFP (His-GFP) (unexposed ∼108 ± 7.69 eggs compared to exposed 18 ± 1.97 eggs) (Clarkson and Saint, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments across multiple genetic backgrounds.

claims.claim: His-GFP flies showed reduced oviposition when exposed to wasps (unexposed ~108 ± 7.69 eggs compared to exposed 18 ± 1.97 eggs).
claims.source: We observed this robust response in at least four different genetic backgrounds including Canton-S (CS), Oregon-R (OreR) (unexposed ∼57 ± 2.84 eggs compared to exposed 13 ± 1.88 eggs on average), w1118 (unexposed ∼25 ± 1.54 eggs compared to exposed ∼1 ± 0.53 egg on average), and transgenic flies carrying Histone H2AvD-GFP (His-GFP) (unexposed ∼108 ± 7.69 eggs compared to exposed 18 ± 1.97 eggs) (Clarkson and Saint, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments across multiple genetic backgrounds.

claims.claim: Oviposition depression in exposed teacher females persisted for an additional 24-hr post wasp exposure (learned depression: 24–48 hr) (35 ± 2.44 compared to 19 ± 1.33 eggs), relative to age-matched, unexposed sibling controls.
claims.source: Oviposition in exposed teacher females was significantly reduced during the 24-hr exposure to wasps (acute depression: 0–24 hr) (53 ± 3.35 compared to 14 ± 1.59 eggs) and this depression persisted for an additional 24-hr post wasp exposure (learned depression: 24–48 hr) (35 ± 2.44 compared to 19 ± 1.33 eggs), relative to age-matched, unexposed sibling controls (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments showing persistence of behavior.

claims.claim: Naive His-GFP student flies decreased oviposition when paired with exposed Canton-S teacher flies (33 ± 2.34 compared to 6 ± 0.86 eggs).
claims.source: Quantification of total GFP and non-GFP embryos deposited during the 24–48 hr after initial teacher exposure to wasps demonstrated that naive His-GFP student flies had also decreased oviposition, relative to His-GFP siblings mixed with unexposed Canton-S flies (33 ± 2.34 compared to 6 ± 0.86 eggs) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result demonstrating social learning.

claims.claim: Naive Canton-S student flies mixed with pre-exposed His-GFP teacher flies exhibited a decrease in oviposition (46 ± 2.48 compared to 14 ± 1.34 eggs).
claims.source: In the reciprocal experiment, naive Canton-S student flies mixed with pre-exposed His-GFP teacher flies also exhibited a decrease in oviposition (46 ± 2.48 compared to 14 ± 1.34 eggs, see Supplementary files 6,7 for all raw egg numbers) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the reciprocal experiment.

claims.claim: The decrease in oviposition of student flies is not due to an effect of the ratio of teacher to student flies.
claims.source: The decrease in oviposition of student flies is not due to an effect of the ratio of teacher to student flies. We tested a 1:1 ratio of 3 exposed female teachers to 3 naive female student flies. This elicited a similar reduction in oviposition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from control experiments testing different ratios.

claims.claim: When we tested a 1:1 ratio of 3 exposed males to 3 naive female student flies, we found no significant decrease in oviposition for students instructed by exposed males.
claims.source: Interestingly, when we tested a 1:1 ratio of 3 exposed males to 3 naive female student flies, we found no significant decrease in oviposition for students instructed by exposed males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H,I).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the role of males in information transfer.

claims.claim: Under these conditions, only females can transmit predator-response information.
claims.source: This suggests that, under these conditions, only females can transmit predator-response information.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the male teacher experiment results.

claims.claim: Males are neither necessary nor sufficient for the information transfer.
claims.source: Males are neither necessary nor sufficient for the information transfer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the male teacher experiment results.

claims.claim: Teacher-instructed student flies were not able to instruct new students, as the naive Canton-S females did not decrease oviposition.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that our teacher-instructed student His-GFP flies were not able to instruct new students, as the naive Canton-S females did not decrease oviposition (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing whether students can become teachers.

claims.claim: Teachers can instruct multiple cohorts of students.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that teachers can instruct multiple cohorts of students, thus, the inability of a student to become a teacher is not due to a limitation in amount a teacher can teach.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from experiments where teachers were paired with multiple student cohorts.

claims.claim: Dissection of ovaries from females having been exposed to wasps for 24 hr revealed a significant increase in the number of egg chambers exhibiting apoptosis relative to unexposed sibling control females.
claims.source: Dissection of ovaries from females having been exposed to wasps for 24 hr revealed a significant increase in the number of egg chambers exhibiting apoptosis relative to unexposed sibling control females (Supplementary file 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from ovary dissection experiments.

claims.claim: The majority of apoptosis was observed at the stage 7/8 egg chamber checkpoint, with almost no apoptosis in region 2/3.
claims.source: Interestingly, the majority of apoptosis was observed at the stage 7/8 egg chamber checkpoint, with almost no apoptosis in region 2/3, as visualized by DNA staining with 4', 6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), suggesting that the pathway through which apoptosis was being triggered is fundamentally different from previously described apoptotic events (Drummond-Barbosa and Spradling, 2001; McCall, 2004) (Supplementary file 1A,B, Figure 4A–F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from microscopy analysis of ovaries, with comparison to previous literature.

claims.claim: The pathway through which apoptosis was being triggered is fundamentally different from previously described apoptotic events.
claims.source: Interestingly, the majority of apoptosis was observed at the stage 7/8 egg chamber checkpoint, with almost no apoptosis in region 2/3, as visualized by DNA staining with 4', 6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), suggesting that the pathway through which apoptosis was being triggered is fundamentally different from previously described apoptotic events (Drummond-Barbosa and Spradling, 2001; McCall, 2004) (Supplementary file 1A,B, Figure 4A–F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the specific stage of apoptosis observed, compared to literature.

claims.claim: Wasp exposure triggered a true apoptotic event as evidenced by the presence of characteristic DAPI-intense pychnotic nurse cell nuclei, by TUNEL stain that detects fragmented DNA, and activated caspase-3 staining.
claims.source: Further confirmation that wasp exposure triggered a true apoptotic event is evidenced by the presence of characteristic DAPI-intense pychnotic nurse cell nuclei, by terminal deoxynucleotide transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) stain that detects fragmented DNA (Figure 4G–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F), and activated caspase-3 staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–J): All positive markers of the cell death process (McCall, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a result from multiple staining methods confirming apoptosis, with citation to established markers.

claims.claim: Physiologically triggered apoptosis specifically of stage 7/8 egg chambers persisted well beyond the period of initial wasp exposure.
claims.source: Similar to the reduced oviposition behavior observed, this physiologically triggered apoptosis specifically of stage 7/8 egg chambers persisted well beyond the period of initial wasp exposure (Figure 4A,B, Supplementary file 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from time-course experiments showing persistence of apoptosis.

claims.claim: Both wasp-exposed and unexposed flies exhibited a similar amount of high-protein yeast food intake.
claims.source: We found that both wasp-exposed and unexposed flies exhibited a similar amount of high-protein yeast food intake even when given a choice to feed on normal food without yeast by visualizing the red dye in the fly abdomens (Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from feeding experiments using dyed food.

claims.claim: Even in the presence of high-protein yeast food, exposed flies still depressed oviposition when compared to unexposed controls, in addition to having apoptosis induced at the egg chamber stage 7/8 checkpoint.
claims.source: We found that even in the presence of high-protein yeast food, exposed flies still depressed oviposition when compared to unexposed controls, in addition to having apoptosis induced at the egg chamber stage 7/8 checkpoint (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1M–T, Supplementary file 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the role of nutrition in oviposition depression.

claims.claim: The mid-oogenesis apoptosis checkpoint triggered in exposed flies is not due to a poor nutrition intake.
claims.source: Thus, the mid-oogenesis apoptosis checkpoint triggered in exposed flies is not due to a poor nutrition intake.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the nutrition experiments.

claims.claim: Naive student flies mixed with exposed teachers showed apoptosis at the stage 7/8 checkpoint, as did their teachers.
claims.source: Naive student flies mixed with exposed teachers showed apoptosis at the stage 7/8 checkpoint, as did their teachers (Supplementary file 1C,D,F,G, Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments examining apoptosis in student flies.

claims.claim: Students mixed with unexposed, 'mock' teachers did not show significant levels of increased apoptosis in the ovary.
claims.source: Students mixed with unexposed, 'mock' teachers did not show significant levels of increased apoptosis in the ovary (Supplementary file 1C,D,F,G, Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from control experiments.

claims.claim: The Drosophila mid-oogenesis checkpoint is known to activate effector caspases Dcp-1 and drice.
claims.source: The Drosophila mid-oogenesis checkpoint is known to activate effector caspases Dcp-1 and drice (McCall, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: RNAi depletion of Dcp-1 or drice reversed both the decrease in oviposition as well as the increase of stage 7/8 egg chamber apoptosis of wasp-exposed females.
claims.source: By using a maternal α-Tubulin > Gal4 driver to express an RNA-hairpin targeting mRNA from each of these genes, we were able to reverse both the decrease in oviposition as well as the increase of stage 7/8 egg chamber apoptosis of wasp-exposed females, while RNAi depletion of these caspases had no effect on oviposition of unexposed females (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: Following wasp exposure, flies depleted of germ line Dcp-1 or drice function were still excellent teachers capable of cueing naive student flies to decrease their oviposition and induce apoptosis at the stage 7/8 mid-oogenesis checkpoint in the students' ovaries.
claims.source: Strikingly, following wasp exposure, flies, depleted of germ line Dcp-1 or drice function, were still excellent teachers capable of cueing naive student flies to decrease their oviposition and induce apoptosis at the stage 7/8 mid-oogenesis checkpoint in the students' ovaries (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 A-B and G, Supplementary file 1I,J).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing whether apoptosis is required for teaching.

claims.claim: The depressed oviposition response can be decoupled from the process required for teacher–student information transfer.
claims.source: The finding that Dcp-1 and drice deficient females incapable of depressing oviposition can nevertheless convey critical cues to naive students demonstrates that the depressed oviposition response can be decoupled from the process required for teacher–student information transfer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the caspase depletion experiments.

claims.claim: Information transfer in this context is not due to secondary effects of ovarian cell death.
claims.source: Thus, information transfer in this context is not due to secondary effects of ovarian cell death.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the caspase depletion experiments.

claims.claim: Dcp-1- and drice-deficient student females could not depress oviposition in response to exposed, wild-type teachers.
claims.source: Interestingly, Dcp-1- and drice-deficient student females could not depress oviposition in response to exposed, wild-type teachers, suggesting that the same effector caspases activated in exposed teachers are also needed for oviposition depression in students (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing caspase requirements in students.

claims.claim: The depressed oviposition in student flies cannot be from simple mimicry.
claims.source: We conclude that the depressed oviposition in student flies cannot be from simple mimicry.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the caspase experiments showing students need apoptosis machinery.

claims.claim: Orco1 flies could respond to wasps and teach student flies.
claims.source: We found that Orco1 flies could respond to wasps and teach student flies (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the role of olfaction.

claims.claim: Orco1 flies as naive students could learn normally from teacher flies.
claims.source: Additionally, Orco1 flies as naive students could learn normally from teacher flies (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the role of olfaction in learning.

claims.claim: Olfaction is not necessary to perceive the wasp threat nor to confer or receive the information during social learning.
claims.source: These data suggest that olfaction is not necessary to perceive the wasp threat nor to confer or receive the information during social learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the Orco mutant experiments.

claims.claim: The ninaBP315 blind females exhibited no initial response to the presence of wasps and were not able to transmit information to naive flies.
claims.source: The ninaBP315 blind females exhibited no initial response to the presence of wasps and were not able to transmit information to naive flies (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the role of vision.

claims.claim: Blind ninaBP315 student flies were unable to learn from teacher flies.
claims.source: In contrast to Orco1 flies, blind ninaBP315 student flies were unable to learn from teacher flies (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the role of vision in learning.

claims.claim: Visual stimuli are responsible for both the acute and learned response.
claims.source: Our ninaBP315 data suggest that visual stimuli are responsible for both the acute and learned response.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the vision mutant experiments.

claims.claim: Performing the entirety of experiment in darkness using Canton-S or His-GFP teachers yielded no response to the presence of wasps and exposed females were not able to transmit information to naive flies.
claims.source: We found that performing the entirety of experiment in darkness using Canton-S or His-GFP teachers yielded no response to the presence of wasps and exposed females were not able to transmit information to naive flies (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments conducted in darkness.

claims.claim: Performing only the wasp exposure period in the dark and the social-learning period in the light again yielded no response to the presence of wasps and these exposed females were not able to transmit information to naive flies.
claims.source: Similarly, performing only the wasp exposure period in the dark and the social-learning period in the light again yielded no response to the presence of wasps and these exposed females were not able to transmit information to naive flies (Figure 8C,D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with partial darkness.

claims.claim: When the wasp exposure period was in the light but the social-learning period was in the dark, teacher flies had both an acute and learned response, but these teachers were not able to transmit information to naive flies.
claims.source: Finally, we performed the wasp exposure period in the light, but moved the teachers paired with students for the social-learning period into the dark (Figure 8E). Here, we find teacher flies had both an acute and learned response, but these teachers were not able to transmit information to naive flies, presumably due to the learning period being in the dark (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with partial darkness.

claims.claim: Both the acute and learned response are intact when performing the exposure in separate, but adjacent, chambers using the Fly Duplex.
claims.source: We find that both the acute and learned response are intact when performing the exposure in separate, but adjacent, chambers using the Fly Duplex (Figure 9B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments using the Fly Duplex apparatus.

claims.claim: Teachers are able to transmit information to naive flies when in separate chambers, yielding depressed oviposition.
claims.source: We also find that teachers are able to transmit information to naive flies when in separate chambers, yielding depressed oviposition (Figure 9B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments using the Fly Duplex apparatus.

claims.claim: Visual cues alone are sufficient for acute-, learned-, and social-learning responses.
claims.source: Both the requirement for light and the use of the Fly Duplex strongly suggest that olfactory, auditory, and tactile information is not likely to be important for this type of social communication. Instead, this demonstrates that visual cues alone are sufficient for acute-, learned-, and social-learning responses.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the Fly Duplex and darkness experiments.

claims.claim: One-winged wg1 flies are unable to act as teachers.
claims.source: We find that both one-winged and two-winged mutants have an intact acute and learned response following wasp exposure (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 10F). However, one-winged wg1 flies are unable to act as teachers, suggesting a role for both wings in communication (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with wingless mutants.

claims.claim: Two-winged wg1 flies behaved as wild-type teachers.
claims.source: Two-winged wg1 flies behaved as wild-type teachers, demonstrating that the wg1 mutation does not induce impaired teaching (Figure 10—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with wingless mutants.

claims.claim: Canton-S flies with mechanically removed wings displayed an intact acute and learned response, but they were unable to teach.
claims.source: The wings of wild-type Canton-S flies were cut prior to wasp exposure and tested for oviposition response. These flies displayed an intact acute and learned response, but they were unable to teach (Figure 10D–F, Figure 10—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with mechanically removed wings.

claims.claim: Flies expressing reaper in the wing disc have an intact acute and learned response, but they were unable to teach.
claims.source: Finally, we used the GAL4/UAS system to express the cell death protein reaper (UAS-Rpr) in conjunction with a wing driver (MS1096) to ablate proper wing development (Figure 10G, Figure 10—figure supplement 1E). We find that these flies also have an intact acute and learned response, but they were unable to teach (Figure 10H).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with genetically ablated wings.

claims.claim: Flies lacking wild-type wings were able to function as students.
claims.source: Flies lacking wild-type wings were able to function as students, demonstrating that wings are not necessary for student learning (Figure 10—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments testing wing requirements for learning.

claims.claim: Both wings and wing movements are necessary for teaching ability.
claims.source: Through the use of multiple genetic mutants and genetic and mechanical perturbations of wings, we find that both wings and wing movements are necessary for teaching ability.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from multiple wing manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Teacher flies are using their wings as the visual cue to inform naive student flies.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that teacher flies are using their wings as the visual cue to inform naive student flies.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the wing manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Learning and memory mutants rutabaga (rut1, rut2080), dunce (dnc1, dncML), Adf1 (Adf1nal), amnesiac (amn1, amnX8), FMR1 (Fmr13, Fmr1B55), and Orb2ΔQ each responded acutely to predator presence with a dramatic decrease in oviposition when in the presence of wasps for the first 24 hr.
claims.source: Each of these mutants responded acutely to predator presence with a dramatic decrease in oviposition when in the presence of wasps for the first 24 hr (Figure 12A,C,E,G,I,K and Figure 12—figure supplement 1A,B,E,G).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with learning and memory mutants.

claims.claim: The acute oviposition depression is independent of learning and memory gene functions.
claims.source: This indicates that the acute oviposition depression is independent of these gene functions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the learning mutant experiments.

claims.claim: When wasps were removed and mutant flies were placed in a new tube for an additional 24 hr after wasp exposure, oviposition returned to levels comparable to unexposed flies.
claims.source: However, when wasps were removed and mutant flies were placed in a new tube for an additional 24 hr after wasp exposure, oviposition returned to levels comparable to unexposed flies (Figure 12A,C,E,G,I,K and Figure 12—figure supplement 1A,B,E,G).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with learning and memory mutants.

claims.claim: The persistence of decreased oviposition behavior after wasp removal requires a form of long-term memory whose consolidation requires cAMP signaling and translational control mediated at least in part through the prion domain of Orb2.
claims.source: This indicates that although the acute response to a predator threat does not require memory consolidation, the persistence of decreased oviposition behavior after wasp removal requires a form of long-term memory whose consolidation requires cAMP signaling and translational control mediated at least in part through the prion domain of Orb2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the learning mutant experiments.

claims.claim: Naive wild-type student flies encountering the pre-exposed mutants did not respond through oviposition decrease.
claims.source: Naive wild-type student flies encountering the pre-exposed mutants also did not respond through oviposition decrease (Figure 12A,C,E,G,I,K and Figure 12—figure supplement 1A,B,E,G).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with learning and memory mutants as teachers.

claims.claim: Socially learned depression of oviposition in naive student flies was defective in rut, dnc, Adf1, amn, FMR1, and Orb2 mutants.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, socially learned depression of oviposition in naive student flies was defective in rut, dnc, Adf1, amn, FMR1, and Orb2 mutants (Figure 12B,D,F,H,J and Figure 12—figure supplement 1C,D,F,H).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments with learning and memory mutants as students.

claims.claim: Wasp-induced and teacher-induced reductions in oviposition behavior occur through fundamentally different mechanisms.
claims.source: As these learning mutants show normal acute oviposition depression in response to direct wasp exposure, this suggests that wasp-induced and teacher-induced reductions in oviposition behavior occur through fundamentally different mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the learning mutant experiments.

claims.claim: The apoptotic response to acute wasp exposure (0–24 hr) in orb2ΔQ was similar to the wild type.
claims.source: The apoptotic response to acute wasp exposure (0–24 hr) in orb2ΔQ was similar to the wild type, as expected, given that these flies had a normal depressed oviposition in presence of wasps (Figure 12M, Supplementary file 1K).
claims.evidence: This is a result from apoptosis analysis in orb2 mutants.

claims.claim: In the 24-hr period following removal of wasps (24–48 hr), orb2ΔQ female flies had increased their egg laying and showed low levels of apoptosis in stage 7/8 egg chambers comparable to control unexposed flies.
claims.source: However, in the 24-hr period following removal of wasps (24–48 hr), orb2ΔQ female flies had increased their egg laying and showed low levels of apoptosis in stage 7/8 egg chambers comparable to control unexposed flies (Figure 12M, Supplementary file 1L).
claims.evidence: This is a result from apoptosis analysis in orb2 mutants.

claims.claim: Decapitated flies could not maintain the same level of reduced oviposition as normal flies and they could no longer teach.
claims.source: We found that decapitated flies could not maintain the same level of reduced oviposition as normal flies (i.e., decapitation led to an increase in oviposition), and they could no longer teach, suggesting a continued input from the brain is needed to elicit these behavioral changes (Figure 13A–C, Figure 13—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from decapitation experiments.

claims.claim: Flies expressing UAS-TeTx in the MB exhibited a wild-type acute response.
claims.source: We found that flies expressing UAS-TeTx in the MB exhibited a wild-type acute response, suggesting that the acute response occurs independent of the MB.
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments blocking synaptic transmission in the mushroom body.

claims.claim: In the learned period, flies expressing UAS-TeTx in the MB no longer showed reduced oviposition and were unable to teach naive students.
claims.source: However, in the learned period, these flies no longer showed reduced oviposition and were unable to teach naive students (Figure 13D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments blocking synaptic transmission in the mushroom body.

claims.claim: Flies expressing UAS-TeTx in the MB failed to function as students.
claims.source: Flies expressing UAS-TeTx in the MB failed to function as students (Figure 13—figure supplement 1J–K).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments blocking synaptic transmission in the mushroom body.

claims.claim: Wasp presence is sensed through the visual system, and this information is relayed to the MB to induce a persistent reduction of oviposition, apoptosis, and teaching behavior.
claims.source: These data suggest that wasp presence is sensed through the visual system, and this information is relayed to the MB to induce a persistent reduction of oviposition, apoptosis, and teaching behavior, all of which are maintained over a time span of days.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the mushroom body manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: RNAi depletion of Orb2 in the MB produced the same phenotype as the orb2ΔQ mutant tested.
claims.source: We found that RNAi depletion of Orb2 in the MB produced the same phenotype as the orb2ΔQ mutant tested (Figure 12A,B, Figure 14A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RNAi experiments targeting orb2 in the mushroom body.

claims.claim: Flies deficient in orb2 in the MB are able to perceive and respond to wasps, but not remember exposure, and therefore cannot teach naive students, once wasps are removed.
claims.source: This result highlights that flies deficient in orb2 in the MB are able to perceive and respond to wasps, but not remember exposure, and therefore cannot teach naive students, once wasps are removed.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the orb2 RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: Flies deficient in orb2 in the MB are also unable to learn from wild-type teachers.
claims.source: Flies deficient in orb2 in the MB are also unable to learn from wild-type teachers.
claims.evidence: This is a result from orb2 RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: Persistence of depressed oviposition behavior likely requires long-term memory formation in the MB.
claims.source: This suggests that orb2 is required in MB neuronal circuits in order for maintained wasp-induced oviposition depression, and it further suggests that persistence of this behavior likely requires long-term memory formation is the MB.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the orb2 RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: Flies expressing the MB Gene-Switch construct and carrying the UAS-Orb2-RNA-hairpin construct, that were not fed RU486, showed normal, wild-type memory, learning, and teaching ability.
claims.source: Flies expressing the MB Gene-Switch and carrying the UAS-Orb2-RNA-hairpin construct, that were not fed RU486, showed normal, wild-type memory, learning, and teaching ability (Figure 16C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from Gene-Switch experiments without RU486.

claims.claim: Flies expressing the MB Gene-Switch and carrying the UAS-Orb2-RNA-hairpin construct, which were fed RU486, showed a wild-type acute response, but impaired memory formation, learning, and teaching abilities.
claims.source: Flies expressing the MB Gene-Switch and carrying the UAS-Orb2-RNA-hairpin construct, which were fed RU486, showed a wild-type acute response, but impaired memory formation, learning, and teaching abilities (Figure 16A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from Gene-Switch experiments with RU486.

claims.claim: Normal orb2 function is required in the adult MB for normal long-term memory formation and behavioral changes that persist over multiple days.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that normal orb2 function is required in the adult MB for normal long-term memory formation and behavioral changes that persist over multiple days, such as the ability to teach.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the Gene-Switch experiments.

claims.claim: Depressed oviposition response can be transmitted from experienced teacher females to naive student females through an independent pathway from ovarian apoptosis.
claims.source: We also find that this behavior can be socially transmitted from experienced teacher females to naive student females: the transfer of information from teachers does not occur as a by-product of apoptosis in the teacher, but rather through an independent pathway, since depressed oviposition is not a necessary condition for social transmission of reduced egg-laying behavior or apoptosis in the student females (Figure 17).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the caspase depletion experiments.

claims.claim: Teacher-instructed students continued to exhibit depressed oviposition and stage 7/8 egg chamber apoptosis in the 24-hr period after removal of teachers.
claims.source: We emphasize that teacher-instructed students continued to exhibit depressed oviposition and stage 7/8 egg chamber apoptosis in the 24-hr period after removal of teachers.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the teacher-student experiments.

claims.claim: Depressed oviposition itself is not sufficient for information transfer.
claims.source: This again indicates that depressed oviposition itself is not sufficient for information transfer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that students cannot become teachers.

claims.claim: Adaptive information transfer cannot spread throughout a population, since only primary teachers are able to transmit the predator-threat information.
claims.source: However, at a higher level, these observations also indicate that such adaptive information transfer cannot spread throughout a population, since only primary teachers are able to transmit the predator-threat information.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that students cannot become teachers.

claims.claim: Parasitoid wasps pose a serious threat to juvenile Drosophila, with infection rates as high as 90% in natural populations.
claims.source: Such wasps pose a serious threat to juvenile Drosophila, with infection rates as high as 90% in natural populations (Janssen et al., 1988; Driessen et al., 1990; Fleury et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: Adult Drosophila have evolved complex behavioral changes to protect their offspring from these predatory wasps, including altered food preference and reduced oviposition rates.
claims.source: Adult Drosophila have evolved complex behavioral changes to protect their offspring from these predatory wasps, including altered food preference and reduced oviposition rates (Lefevre et al., 2012; Kacsoh et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: Adult Drosophila themselves are not infected by these wasps.
claims.source: Adult Drosophila themselves are not infected by these wasps, thus, making the change in reproductive behavior beneficial only to an anticipated threat to their offspring and not a response to predation itself.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the wasp-fly interaction.

claims.claim: Female Drosophila never having seen this predator can nevertheless robustly and reproducibly respond to it, suggesting an innate recognition of this predator-threat.
claims.source: A remarkable feature of this altered reproductive behavior is that female Drosophila never having seen this predator can nevertheless robustly and reproducibly respond to it, suggesting an innate recognition of this predator-threat.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experiments suggesting innate recognition.

results.result: Drosophila females exhibit acute oviposition depression when exposed to parasitoid wasps, with egg-laying reduced by approximately 70-95% across multiple genetic backgrounds. This depression persists for 24 hours after wasp removal (learned response), and is mediated through the visual system.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C10-C14 provide consistent quantitative evidence across multiple genetic backgrounds (Canton-S, Oregon-R, w1118, His-GFP) showing significant oviposition reduction during wasp exposure (acute response) and persistence after removal (learned response). The data are replicated across different time points and genetic backgrounds, with appropriate controls and statistical significance reported.

results.result: Wasp-exposed teacher flies can socially transmit oviposition depression and ovarian apoptosis to naive student flies. Students paired with exposed teachers show reduced egg-laying (70-80% reduction) and increased stage 7/8 egg chamber apoptosis, while students paired with unexposed teachers show no such effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C15, C16, C31, C32 demonstrate social transmission with quantitative data from reciprocal experiments (Canton-S/His-GFP crosses) and appropriate controls. The use of GFP-marked embryos allows unambiguous discrimination between teacher and student eggs, strengthening the evidence for social learning.

results.result: Teacher-instructed student flies cannot become secondary teachers, though primary teachers can instruct multiple cohorts of students. This demonstrates that social transmission is limited to one generation and that depressed oviposition itself is not sufficient for teaching ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C81-C83 provide clear experimental evidence that students maintain learned behavior but cannot transmit it to new naive flies, while primary teachers can teach multiple cohorts. This establishes an important constraint on information spread and rules out simple mimicry as the mechanism.

results.result: Wasp exposure triggers stage-specific apoptosis at the mid-oogenesis checkpoint (stage 7/8 egg chambers) rather than at region 2/3, confirmed by DAPI staining, TUNEL, and activated caspase-3. This apoptosis persists beyond the initial exposure period and represents a pathway distinct from previously described nutritional stress-induced apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 provide multiple independent markers of apoptosis (DAPI, TUNEL, caspase-3) all showing stage 7/8 specificity. The comparison to literature on nutritional stress (C24, C25) appropriately contextualizes the finding. However, the claim that the pathway is "fundamentally different" (C25) is somewhat speculative without direct mechanistic comparison.

results.result: The mid-oogenesis apoptosis and oviposition depression in wasp-exposed flies is not due to reduced nutrient intake. Both exposed and unexposed flies consume similar amounts of high-protein yeast food, yet exposed flies still show depressed oviposition and stage 7/8 apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide direct experimental evidence using dyed food to visualize consumption. The control experiment effectively rules out nutritional stress as the mechanism, though the sample size (n=3 replicates) is modest. The conclusion is appropriately limited to the experimental conditions tested.

results.result: RNAi depletion of effector caspases Dcp-1 and drice in teachers prevents their own oviposition depression but does not impair their ability to teach students. However, caspase-deficient students cannot learn from wild-type teachers, demonstrating that teaching ability is decoupled from the teacher's physiological response and that learning is not simple mimicry.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 provide strong genetic evidence using RNAi and multiple Dcp-1 alleles. The key finding that caspase-deficient teachers can still teach (C35) while caspase-deficient students cannot learn (C38) is logically sound and rules out mimicry (C39). Control parental lines showed wild-type behavior, strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: Olfaction is not required for perceiving wasp threat or for social learning. Orco1 mutant flies (lacking functional olfactory receptors) can respond to wasps, teach students, and learn from teachers normally.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 provide clear genetic evidence using Orco1 mutants tested in both teacher and student roles. The conclusion is appropriately limited to the experimental conditions, though it would be strengthened by testing additional olfactory mutants.

results.result: Vision is essential for both acute and learned responses to wasps, as well as for social learning. Blind ninaBP315 mutants cannot respond to wasps or teach/learn. Experiments in darkness abolish all responses, while physical separation using the Fly Duplex (allowing only visual cues) preserves all responses, demonstrating that visual cues alone are sufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C51 provide convergent evidence from genetic (ninaBP315), environmental (darkness), and physical (Fly Duplex) manipulations. The Fly Duplex experiments (C49-C50) are particularly strong, ruling out olfactory, auditory, and tactile cues. The systematic testing of different light/dark combinations (C46-C48) effectively dissects the requirements for each phase.

results.result: Both wings and wing movements are necessary for teaching ability but not for learning. One-winged wg1 mutants, flies with mechanically removed wings, and flies with genetically ablated wings (MS1096>UAS-Rpr) all show intact acute and learned responses but cannot teach students. Wingless flies can function as students normally.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 provide convergent evidence from genetic (wg1), mechanical (wing clipping), and developmental (reaper expression) manipulations. The finding that two-winged wg1 flies teach normally (C53) controls for genetic background effects. The conclusion that wings are used as visual cues (C58) is reasonable but somewhat inferential.

results.result: Learning and memory mutants (rutabaga, dunce, Adf1, amnesiac, FMR1, Orb2ΔQ) show normal acute oviposition depression but fail to maintain the response after wasp removal. These mutants also cannot teach students, and wild-type students cannot learn from these mutant teachers, indicating that persistence requires long-term memory consolidation involving cAMP signaling and Orb2-mediated translational control.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 provide systematic genetic evidence across multiple learning/memory genes with consistent phenotypes. The dissociation between acute (intact) and learned (impaired) responses is clear. However, the claim that wasp-induced and teacher-induced responses occur through "fundamentally different mechanisms" (C65) is somewhat overstated—they may share components but have different sensory inputs.

results.result: orb2ΔQ mutants show normal acute apoptosis during wasp exposure but return to baseline apoptosis levels 24 hours after wasp removal, paralleling their behavioral recovery. This demonstrates that Orb2 is required for maintaining the physiological response as well as the behavioral response.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 provide direct physiological evidence linking the behavioral and apoptotic phenotypes in orb2 mutants. The parallel between behavior and physiology strengthens the overall model, though the sample size (n=3 replicates) is modest.

results.result: Continued neural input from the mushroom body (MB) is required for learned oviposition depression and teaching. Decapitated flies cannot maintain reduced oviposition or teach. Flies expressing tetanus toxin in the MB (blocking synaptic transmission) show normal acute responses but fail to maintain learned responses, teach, or learn as students.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide convergent evidence from surgical (decapitation) and genetic (UAS-TeTx with OK107-GAL4 and MB247-GAL4) manipulations. The dissociation between acute (MB-independent) and learned (MB-dependent) responses is clear. Control parental lines showed wild-type behavior. The conclusion (C72) appropriately integrates the findings.

results.result: RNAi depletion of Orb2 specifically in the MB recapitulates the orb2ΔQ mutant phenotype: normal acute response but impaired memory, teaching, and learning. This demonstrates that Orb2 function in the MB is necessary for persistent behavioral responses and suggests that long-term memory formation in the MB underlies the learned response.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 provide tissue-specific genetic evidence using the GAL4/UAS system. The phenocopy of the orb2ΔQ mutant by MB-specific RNAi (C73) is strong evidence for MB localization of function. Control lines (OK107-GAL4 alone, UAS-Orb2-RNAi alone) showed wild-type behavior, strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: Adult-specific RNAi depletion of Orb2 in the MB using the Gene-Switch system impairs memory formation, learning, and teaching when RU486 is administered, but not when RU486 is withheld. This demonstrates that Orb2 function is required in the adult MB (not just during development) for long-term memory and persistent behavioral changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 provide temporal control using the Gene-Switch system, effectively ruling out developmental effects. The RU486-dependent phenotype (C78) with normal behavior without RU486 (C77) is strong evidence for adult-specific requirements. Control experiments with white RNAi showed no effects, confirming specificity.

results.result: Long-term persistence of oviposition depression requires neuronal signaling, a functional mushroom body, and neurally driven apoptosis through effector caspases. Social learning by students requires all the same factors as primary learning, but teaching ability is independent of ovarian apoptosis in the teacher.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C8, and C80 synthesize findings from multiple experimental approaches (caspase RNAi, MB manipulations, learning mutants). The evidence for each component is strong, though these claims are somewhat redundant with more detailed results already evaluated. The integration is appropriate.

results.result: The teacher-to-student ratio does not affect social learning efficiency (1:1 ratio works as well as 5:1). Males cannot transmit predator-response information to female students, indicating that only females can teach under these conditions and that males are neither necessary nor sufficient for information transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 provide clear experimental evidence from ratio and sex-specific experiments. The conclusion that males cannot teach (C18) is well-supported, though the interpretation that "only females can transmit" (C19) should be qualified as applying to these specific experimental conditions.

results.result: Parasitoid wasps pose a serious ecological threat to Drosophila larvae (up to 90% infection rates in nature), and adult flies have evolved behavioral responses including reduced oviposition. Adult flies are not themselves infected, making this an anticipatory response. Naive flies respond robustly to wasps, suggesting innate recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 provide appropriate ecological context from the literature (C84-C85) and established knowledge about the wasp-fly interaction (C86). The observation of innate recognition (C87) is supported by the experimental data showing naive flies respond to first exposure, though the claim is somewhat inferential.
